chapter_note.about: Sets and logic are the grammar of discrete mathematics, and they return in databases, probability and AI. This chapter builds seven ideas from nothing: sets and subsets, union and intersection, counting with Venn diagrams, AND, OR and NOT, implication, De Morgan and equivalences, and quantifiers. Each card starts from a picture, such as a Venn diagram, a truth table or a row of in/out switches, and ends with a question shaped like GATE. Union, intersection and complement mirror OR, AND and NOT exactly, so each half of the chapter helps the other.
chapter_note.simple: A set is a bag of different things, and a Venn diagram draws each bag as a circle so you can see what overlaps. Logic is about statements that are true or false. 'And' needs both parts true, 'or' needs at least one, and 'not' flips the answer. 'If p then q' is a promise that is broken only when p happens and q does not. 'For all' means every single one, 'there exists' means at least one, and to break an 'every' claim you only need one counterexample. Sets and logic are the same game in two outfits: union is 'or', overlap is 'and', and the outside of a circle is 'not'.

cards.title: Sets, membership and subsets
cards.simple: A set is a collection of different things, like the songs on a playlist or the players in a cricket team. The order does not matter and repeats do not count. You write it in curly brackets, such as $\{a,b,c\}$. The symbol $\in$ means 'is one of the items', so $a\in\{a,b,c\}$. A subset is a smaller collection built only from items of the big one, like a 3-song playlist taken from a 10-song one. To count the subsets of a set with 3 items, decide for each item 'in or out': that is $2\times2\times2=8$ choices. In exam words: $x\in A$ is membership, $B\subseteq A$ is subset, and a set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets.
cards.idea: A **set** is a collection of distinct items, written in curly brackets, where order and repeats do not matter. The symbol $\in$ says an item is **in** a set. A set $B$ is a **subset** of $A$ when every item of $B$ is also in $A$. The empty set $\emptyset$ has no items and is a subset of every set.
cards.definition:
$$x\in A,\qquad B\subseteq A,\qquad |A|=\text{number of elements},\qquad |\mathcal P(A)|=2^{|A|}$$

$x\in A$ means $x$ is one of the items of $A$. $B\subseteq A$ means every item of $B$ is in $A$. $|A|$ is the size of $A$. The **power set** $\mathcal P(A)$ is the set of all subsets of $A$, and it has $2^{|A|}$ elements. The **empty set** $\emptyset=\{\}$ has size 0. Note that $\emptyset\ne\{\emptyset\}$, because the second set has one item.
cards.intuition_full: Think of a set as a bag and ignore the order of what is inside. $\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{3,1,2\}$ are the same bag, and listing 2 twice changes nothing. $\in$ talks about a single thing inside the bag, while $\subseteq$ talks about a smaller bag that fits inside it. So $2\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{2\}\subseteq\{1,2,3\}$, but $2\subseteq\{1,2,3\}$ is meaningless because 2 is not a bag. The count of subsets comes from in/out switches. Each element has a switch, and a subset is one setting of all the switches. Three switches have $2^3=8$ settings. Building up one element at a time shows the doubling. With no elements there is one subset, $\emptyset$. Adding $a$ lets every old subset either leave $a$ out or take it in, which gives 2. Adding $b$ gives 4, and adding $c$ gives 8. Every new element doubles the count. A set can contain sets: $S=\{1,\{2,3\}\}$ has just 2 elements, the number 1 and the set $\{2,3\}$. A database table is a set of rows, and a relation is a set of pairs, so these ideas return again and again.

examples.setup: List all subsets of $\{a,b,c\}$ and count them.
steps: Start with no elements. The only subset is $\emptyset$. Count 1.
Add $a$. Every old subset can leave $a$ out or take it in: $\emptyset$ and $\{a\}$. Count 2.
Add $b$. Each old subset can leave $b$ out or take it in: $\emptyset,\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b\}$. Count 4.
Add $c$ the same way. Copy the 4 subsets and put $c$ into each copy: $\{c\},\{a,c\},\{b,c\},\{a,b,c\}$. Count 8.
Each of the 3 elements is in or out, so the count is $2\times2\times2=2^3=8$.
examples.answer: 8 subsets: the 4 without $c$ and the 4 with $c$.

examples.setup: How many binary relations are there on a 3-element set $A$?
steps: A relation on $A$ is any subset of $A\times A$, a set of ordered pairs.
$|A\times A|=3\times3=9$ pairs.
A subset of a 9-element set: each pair is in or out, so $2^9$ subsets.
Small check: for a 1-element set, $A\times A$ has 1 pair and $2^1=2$ relations (empty, or the one pair).
examples.answer: 512 relations. The trap avoided: using $2^3=8$ instead of $2^{3\times3}$.

examples.setup: Let $S=\{1,\{2,3\}\}$. Find $|S|$. Which of these are true: $2\in S$, $\{2,3\}\in S$, $\{2,3\}\subseteq S$, $\{\{2,3\}\}\subseteq S$?
steps: The items of $S$ are the number 1 and the set $\{2,3\}$, so $|S|=2$.
$2\in S$? The number 2 is inside the inner set, not an item of $S$. False.
$\{2,3\}\in S$? It is one of the two items. True.
$\{2,3\}\subseteq S$ would need 2 and 3 to be items of $S$. They are not. False.
$\{\{2,3\}\}\subseteq S$: its only item, $\{2,3\}$, is in $S$. True.
examples.answer: $|S|=2$. True: $\{2,3\}\in S$ and $\{\{2,3\}\}\subseteq S$. False: $2\in S$ and $\{2,3\}\subseteq S$.

edge_cases: $\emptyset\subseteq A$ for every set $A$, including $A=\emptyset$.
$\emptyset\ne\{\emptyset\}$: the first has 0 elements and the second has 1.
Repeats do not count: $\{1,1,2\}=\{1,2\}$ has size 2.
$A\subseteq A$ always. A subset that is not the whole set is called a proper subset.

cards.title: Union, intersection, difference and complement
cards.simple: Think of two friend groups at school. Group A plays cricket, group B plays football, and some kids are in both. The union is everybody who plays at least one of the games. The intersection is only the kids who play both. The difference $A-B$ is the cricket-only kids. The complement $A'$ is everyone in school who does not play cricket. A Venn diagram draws each group as a circle, so you can point at the region you mean. In exam words: $A\cup B$, $A\cap B$, $A-B$ and $A'$ are union, intersection, difference and complement, taken inside a universal set $U$.
cards.idea: Sets combine in four basic ways, and each one is a region of a Venn diagram. The **union** $A\cup B$ keeps what is in at least one of them, and the **intersection** $A\cap B$ keeps what they share. The **difference** $A-B$ keeps what is in $A$ but not in $B$. The **complement** $A'$ keeps everything in the universe $U$ that is not in $A$.
cards.definition:
$$A\cup B=\{x: x\in A\text{ or }x\in B\},\qquad A\cap B=\{x: x\in A\text{ and }x\in B\}$$
$$A-B=\{x: x\in A\text{ and }x\notin B\},\qquad A'=U-A$$

$U$ is the **universal set**, the box that holds everything under discussion. Two sets are **disjoint** when $A\cap B=\emptyset$. The symmetric difference $A\,\Delta\,B=(A-B)\cup(B-A)$ is the 'exactly one' region.
cards.intuition_full: Words and symbols line up: 'or' is $\cup$, 'and' is $\cap$, 'not' is the complement, 'but not' is the difference. Drawing the picture is the fastest check. Put $U$ as a box and two overlapping circles inside it. That makes four regions: only $A$, both, only $B$, and neither. The union is the three regions inside the circles. The intersection is the lens in the middle. $A-B$ is the part of circle $A$ outside the lens. The complement $A'$ is the whole box minus circle $A$, so it includes the 'only $B$' region and 'neither'. A complement only has meaning relative to a universe. If $U=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ then $\{1,2\}'=\{3,4,5\}$, but inside $U=\{1,2,3\}$ the same set has complement $\{3\}$. The symmetric difference is the 'exactly one' region and matches the XOR of logic.

steps: Draw $U$ as a box and $A$, $B$ as overlapping circles. 1 and 2 are only in $A$, 3 and 4 are in both, 5 and 6 are only in $B$, and 7, 8, 9 are outside both circles.
Union $A\cup B$: everything inside either circle, $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$.
Intersection $A\cap B$: only the overlap, $\{3,4\}$.
Difference $A-B$: inside $A$ but not in the overlap, $\{1,2\}$.
Complement $A'$: everything in the box outside circle $A$, $\{5,6,7,8,9\}$.
$A-B$: in $A$ and not in $B$, so $\{1,2,3\}$.
$A\cap B=\{4,5,6\}$ has size 3. The formula gives $6+5-2\times3=5$, which agrees.
The shared elements are removed from both sides, which is why the overlap is subtracted twice.
The same set $A$ has two different complements. The complement depends on the universe, so always know $U$.

how: Draw the universe box and the circles.
Match each word to a region: or, and, not, but-not.
Fill each region with the elements that belong there.
Read off the set, or its size, from the chosen regions.
For complements, check which universe the question uses.
cards.mistake: Reading 'or' as 'one or the other' for the union. In maths $A\cup B$ includes the overlap. Another slip is forgetting that $A'$ contains the elements of $B$ that are not in $A$: the complement is taken in $U$, not only inside $B$.
edge_cases: $A\cup\emptyset=A$ and $A\cap\emptyset=\emptyset$.
$A\cup A'=U$ and $A\cap A'=\emptyset$.
If $A\subseteq B$ then $A\cup B=B$ and $A\cap B=A$.
$A-B$ and $B-A$ are usually different: difference is not symmetric.
connections: Used in: Probability. Events are sets: 'A or B' is $A\cup B$, 'A and B' is $A\cap B$, 'not A' is $A'$ (prob.axioms).
Used in: Databases. Relational algebra has union, intersection and set difference on tables (db.relalg).
Used in: Logic (cards 4 to 6). Union is OR, intersection is AND, complement is NOT.

cards.title: Counting with Venn diagrams
cards.simple: Count the kids who like tea and the kids who like coffee, then add the two numbers. The kids who like both got counted twice, once in each group. To fix it, take away the 'both' group once. That single correction is the whole idea of inclusion-exclusion. A Venn diagram makes it visible: each circle is a group, and the overlap is where you double counted. To find the kids who like neither, subtract the people in at least one circle from the whole class. In exam words: $|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|$, and for three sets you add the triple overlap back at the end.
cards.idea: When you add the sizes of two sets, anything in both sets is counted **twice**. Subtract the overlap once to fix it: $|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|$. For three sets, add the sizes, subtract the three pair-overlaps, and add back the triple overlap. People outside every circle are found by subtracting the union from the whole group.
cards.definition:
$$|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|$$
$$|A\cup B\cup C|=|A|+|B|+|C|-|A\cap B|-|B\cap C|-|A\cap C|+|A\cap B\cap C|$$

$|X|$ is the number of elements of $X$. Those in neither set number $|U|-|A\cup B|$. With probabilities in place of counts the same rule reads $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$.
cards.intuition_full: Fill the Venn diagram from the inside out. The overlap is the first number to find, because it sits inside both circles. Each circle's total includes the overlap, so 'only $A$' is $|A|-|A\cap B|$ and 'only $B$' is $|B|-|A\cap B|$. Adding the three separate regions (only $A$, both, only $B$) gives the union, and it simplifies to $|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|$. For three sets, a person in all three circles is added 3 times by the single sizes, subtracted 3 times by the pair overlaps, and so ends at 0. Adding the triple overlap back once puts them at exactly 1. The pattern of signs is plus, minus, plus. If the sets are disjoint, the overlap is 0 and the union is just the sum. If one set sits inside another, the union is the bigger one.

examples.setup: In a class of 40 students, 25 play cricket, 18 play football and 8 play both. How many play at least one game, and how many play neither?
steps: Draw a box of 40 students with two circles. Start in the overlap: 8 play both.
Cricket has 25 in total, and 8 of them sit in the overlap. Cricket only: $25-8=17$.
Football only: $18-8=10$.
At least one game: $17+8+10=35$. The shortcut gives the same: $25+18-8=35$.
Neither: $40-35=5$, the students outside both circles.
examples.answer: 35 play at least one game and 5 play neither.

examples.setup: In a survey of 120 people, 60 read paper $A$, 50 read $B$ and 40 read $C$. Also 20 read both $A$ and $B$, 15 read both $B$ and $C$, 12 read both $A$ and $C$, and 8 read all three. How many read none?
steps: Add the singles: $60+50+40=150$.
Subtract the pair overlaps: $20+15+12=47$, so $150-47=103$.
Add back the triple overlap: $103+8=111$ read at least one.
examples.answer: 9 people read none.

examples.setup: $|A|=30$, $|B|=35$ and $|A\cup B|=50$. Find $|A\cap B|$, the number only in $A$, and the number only in $B$.
steps: Rearrange the formula: $|A\cap B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cup B|=30+35-50=15$.
examples.answer: Overlap 15, only $A$ 15, only $B$ 20.

cards.why: Counting 'at least one', 'exactly one' or 'none' in a group is a standard General Aptitude and discrete-maths question. The same formula, with probabilities in place of counts, is the addition rule of probability. In GATE: two- and three-set Venn problems, 'neither' counts, and $P(A\cup B)$.
how: Draw the circles and write the known overlap first.
Subtract the overlap from each total to get the 'only' regions.
Add the separate regions to get the union.
Subtract the union from the total for 'none'.
For three sets: add the singles, subtract the pairs, add the triple.
cards.mistake: Adding the two set sizes and stopping, or forgetting to add back the triple overlap in a three-set problem. The sum $|A|+|B|$ counts the overlap twice. A sign of this slip: the union comes out larger than the whole group.
edge_cases: Disjoint sets: the overlap is 0, so the union is just $|A|+|B|$.
If $A\subseteq B$, the overlap equals $|A|$ and the union is $|B|$.
The overlap is at most the smaller set: $|A\cap B|\le\min(|A|,|B|)$.
'Exactly one' is $|A|+|B|-2|A\cap B|$.
connections: Used in: Probability. $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ is the same formula (prob.axioms).
Used in: Counting. Inclusion-exclusion counts derangements and numbers coprime to $n$ (dm.counting).
Used in: General Aptitude. Survey and 'how many like neither' puzzles.

**Worked example.** In a class of 40 students, 25 play cricket, 18 play football and 8 play both. How many play at least one game, and how many play neither?

1. Draw a box of 40 students with two circles. Start in the overlap: 8 play both.
2. Cricket has 25 in total, and 8 of them sit in the overlap. Cricket only: $25-8=17$.
3. Football only: $18-8=10$.
4. At least one game: $17+8+10=35$. The shortcut gives the same: $25+18-8=35$.
5. Neither: $40-35=5$, the students outside both circles.

**Answer:** 35 play at least one game and 5 play neither.

cards.title: Propositions and AND, OR, NOT
cards.simple: A statement that is either true or false, like 'it is raining' or '7 is even', is called a proposition. Logic joins statements the way English joins words. 'And' is true only if both parts are true, like needing both your ticket and your ID to enter a hall. 'Or' is true if at least one part is true, like being allowed in with either a ticket or an invitation. 'Not' flips a statement from true to false. A truth table lists every possible combination of true and false for the parts and shows the result of the whole sentence in each case. In exam words: $p\wedge q$ is conjunction, $p\vee q$ is (inclusive) disjunction, $\neg p$ is negation, and $n$ statements give $2^n$ rows.
cards.idea: A **proposition** is a statement that is exactly true or false. **AND** ($\wedge$) is true only when both parts are true, **OR** ($\vee$) is true when at least one part is true, and **NOT** ($\neg$) flips true to false. A **truth table** lists every combination of the parts and the result of the whole in each case.
cards.definition:
$$\neg p,\qquad p\wedge q,\qquad p\vee q$$

For two propositions there are 4 rows. $p\wedge q$ is true in 1 of them (both true), $p\vee q$ is false in only 1 (both false), and $\neg p$ has the opposite value of $p$. With $n$ propositions the table has $2^n$ rows. The 'exclusive or' $p\oplus q$ is true when **exactly one** of the two is true.
cards.intuition_full: Logic is the arithmetic of true and false. AND behaves like multiplying 1 (true) and 0 (false): $1\times1=1$, and anything times 0 is 0. OR behaves like 'at least one', so it fails only if every part fails. NOT swaps 1 and 0. Everyday English hides a trap. 'Tea or coffee' on a menu usually means one of the two, but in logic $\vee$ is inclusive, so it also allows both. When you need 'exactly one', use XOR. To build a truth table, list the rows in a fixed order: for 3 variables write TTT, TTF, TFT, and so on, so you get all $2^3=8$ without missing or repeating one. For a longer expression, add a column for each sub-expression and work from the inside out. The fastest way to count rows is to find where the expression fails (for OR) or holds (for AND), since each is a single case.

cards.title: Implication: if p then q
cards.simple: Think of a promise: 'If it rains, I will carry an umbrella.' When is the promise broken? Only if it rains and I walk out without an umbrella. If it is sunny, I have not broken anything, whether I carry an umbrella or not. That is exactly how logic treats 'if p then q': it is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false. The reverse sentence, 'if I carry an umbrella then it rains', says something different and is not the same promise. But 'if I have no umbrella then it is not raining' is the same promise in disguise. In exam words: $p\to q$ is false only for $p=T$, $q=F$; the converse $q\to p$ is not equivalent; the contrapositive $\neg q\to\neg p$ is equivalent.
cards.idea: **Implication** $p\to q$ ('if $p$ then $q$') is a promise. It is broken in exactly one case: $p$ is true and $q$ is false. When $p$ is false nothing was promised, so the statement counts as true. Flipping and negating both parts gives the **contrapositive** $\neg q\to\neg p$, which always has the same truth value.
cards.definition:
$$p\to q\ \equiv\ \neg p\vee q$$

$p\to q$ is false only when $p=T$ and $q=F$. Related statements:

- **Converse**: $q\to p$ (not equivalent).
- **Inverse**: $\neg p\to\neg q$ (not equivalent).
- **Contrapositive**: $\neg q\to\neg p$ (equivalent to $p\to q$).
- **Biconditional** $p\leftrightarrow q$: true when $p$ and $q$ have the same value, equal to $(p\to q)\wedge(q\to p)$.

A rule 'if $p$ then $q$' is only tested when $p$ happens. On a dry day nobody can say the umbrella promise was broken, so the rule survives, and logic calls it true. This is called vacuous truth. 'If $1>2$ then pigs fly' is true for this reason, and so is 'every student in an empty room is a genius': there is no one to prove it wrong. The formula $
eg p\vee q$ says the same thing in other words: either $p$ is false (no promise was tested) or $q$ is true (the promise was kept). The contrapositive follows the same logic. If $q$ is false and the rule holds, $p$ cannot have happened, so $
eg q	o
eg p$. The converse $q	o p$ answers a different question. The rule 'if it rained then the pavement is wet' does not give 'if the pavement is wet then it rained', because a tap could have wet it. Mixing up the converse with the original is the most common logic error. Proofs by contrapositive use the equivalence to turn a hard 'if $p$ then $q$' into an easier 'if not $q$ then not $p$'.

examples.answer: $p\to q$ is T, F, T, T for the rows TT, TF, FT, FF, which equals $\neg p\vee q$.

Inverse $\neg p\to\neg q$: 'if $n$ is not a multiple of 4 then $n$ is odd'. False: $n=2$ again.
Contrapositive $\neg q\to\neg p$: 'if $n$ is odd then $n$ is not a multiple of 4'. True, like the original.
examples.answer: The original and the contrapositive are true. The converse and the inverse are false.

Second: $p$ = '$3=3$' is true and $q$ = '$2+2=5$' is false. That is the one broken row, so it is false.
A false 'if' part makes the whole implication true, whatever follows.
examples.answer: The first is true. The second is false.

cards.simple:
Two sentences are equivalent when they mean exactly the same thing, even if they look different. 'It is not true that I like tea or coffee' means 'I do not like tea and I do not like coffee'. Notice that the 'or' became 'and' when the 'not' moved inside. That swap is called De Morgan's law, and it works every time. It works for groups of things too. Everyone outside the union of two clubs is outside the first club and outside the second. In exam words: $
eg(p\vee q)\equiv

eg q$ and $
eg(p\wedge q)\equiv
eg p\vee
eg q$, and for sets $(A\cup B)'=A'\cap B'$ and $(A\cap B)'=A'\cup B'$.

The Venn picture agrees: the outside of the union of two circles is the region outside the first circle AND outside the second. Equivalences are the algebra of logic, since you can replace any piece by an equivalent piece. The useful rules are double negation, De Morgan, the implication rewrite $p\to q\equiv\neg p\vee q$, distribution ($p\wedge(q\vee r)\equiv(p\wedge q)\vee(p\wedge r)$) and the two shortcuts above. When a long formula refuses to simplify, build its truth table. The result is a small column of T and F that you can match against known forms. Two formulas are equivalent exactly when joining them with $\leftrightarrow$ gives a tautology.

A **tautology** is true in every row and a **contradiction** is false in every row. To check an equivalence, compare truth tables, or rewrite step by step with these laws. Two handy shortcuts are $p\vee(p\wedge q)\equiv p$ and $p\vee(\neg p\wedge q)\equiv p\vee q$.

**Worked example.** Let $U=\{1,\ldots,8\}$, $A=\{1,2,3\}$ and $B=\{3,4,5\}$. Check that $(A\cap B)'=A'\cup B'$.

1. Draw the Venn diagram: 1 and 2 are only in $A$, 3 is in both, 4 and 5 are only in $B$, and 6, 7, 8 are outside both circles.
2. $A\cap B=\{3\}$, so $(A\cap B)'$ is everything except 3: $\{1,2,4,5,6,7,8\}$.
3. $A'=\{4,5,6,7,8\}$ (outside circle $A$).
4. $B'=\{1,2,6,7,8\}$ (outside circle $B$).
5. $A'\cup B'=\{1,2,4,5,6,7,8\}$, the same set as in step 2. In logic: $\neg(p\wedge q)\equiv\neg p\vee\neg q$.

**Answer:** Both sides equal $\{1,2,4,5,6,7,8\}$, so De Morgan holds.

Equivalences let you simplify conditions, negate statements correctly, and convert formulas into the standard forms that circuits and automated provers use. In GATE: simplifying a formula, choosing the equivalent of a negated statement, and recognising tautologies.

cards.title: Quantifiers: for all and there exists
cards.simple:
A quantifier says how many things a statement is about. 'For all' ($ orall$) means every single one, as in 'every student in this class has a phone'. One student without a phone breaks it. 'There exists' ($\exists$) means at least one, as in 'some student has a phone'. One student with a phone is enough. To show a 'for all' statement is false you only need one counterexample, so the opposite of 'everyone has a phone' is 'someone has no phone', not 'no one has a phone'. Order matters too: 'everyone has a friend' is not the same as 'someone is everyone's friend'. In exam words: $
eg orall x\,P(x)\equiv\exists x\,
eg P(x)$, $
eg\exists x\,P(x)\equiv orall x\,
eg P(x)$, and swapping $ orall$ and $\exists$ changes the meaning.
cards.idea: A **predicate** $P(x)$ is a statement about a variable $x$, such as '$x$ is even'. The quantifier $\forall x$ ('for all') claims $P(x)$ holds for **every** $x$ in the domain. The quantifier $\exists x$ ('there exists') claims it holds for **at least one** $x$. To negate a quantified statement, flip the quantifier and negate what is inside.
cards.definition:
$$ orall x\,P(x),\qquad \exists x\,P(x)$$
$$
eg orall x\,P(x)\equiv\exists x\,
eg P(x),\qquad 
eg\exists x\,P(x)\equiv orall x\,
eg P(x)$$

The **domain** is the set of values $x$ may take. Standard translations: 'all $A$ are $B$' is $ orall x\,(A(x)	o B(x))$, and 'some $A$ is $B$' is $\exists x\,(A(x)\wedge B(x))$. Quantifiers of different kinds do not commute: $ orall x\,\exists y$ is not the same as $\exists y\, orall x$.
cards.intuition_full: Over a finite domain, $\forall$ is a big AND and $\exists$ is a big OR. Over $\{1,2,3\}$, $\forall x\,P(x)$ means $P(1)\wedge P(2)\wedge P(3)$ and $\exists x\,P(x)$ means $P(1)\vee P(2)\vee P(3)$. De Morgan then explains the negation rules: the negation of a big AND is a big OR of negations, so $\neg\forall$ becomes $\exists\neg$. The translation patterns follow the same logic. 'All cats are mammals' must say: for every $x$, if $x$ is a cat then $x$ is a mammal. Using AND would claim that everything is a cat. 'Some cat is black' must say: there is an $x$ that is a cat AND black. An arrow is too weak here, because $\exists x\,(\mathrm{Cat}(x)\to\mathrm{Black}(x))$ is true whenever anything is not a cat, since the arrow is then vacuously true. Finally, read nested quantifiers left to right as a game. In $\forall x\,\exists y$, the opponent picks $x$ and you answer with a $y$ that may depend on $x$. In $\exists y\,\forall x$ you must pick one $y$ that works against every $x$.

examples.setup: The domain is $\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $P(x)$ means '$x$ is even'. Decide $\exists x\,P(x)$ and $\forall x\,P(x)$, then negate the second.
steps: The domain has four elements. $P(x)$ is true for 2 and 4, false for 1 and 3.
$\exists x\,P(x)$: look for one element with $P$. Check 1: no. Check 2: yes. Found one, so it is true.
$\forall x\,P(x)$: every element must satisfy $P$. Check 1: it is odd. One failure is enough, so it is false.
Negation: $\neg\forall x\,P(x)\equiv\exists x\,\neg P(x)$, meaning some element is not even. The witnesses are 1 and 3.
Rule: flip $\forall$ and $\exists$ and negate inside. The same works for $\neg\exists x\,P(x)\equiv\forall x\,\neg P(x)$.
examples.answer: $\exists x\,P(x)$ is true, $\forall x\,P(x)$ is false, and its negation $\exists x\,\neg P(x)$ is true.

examples.setup: Three people $a,b,c$. 'x likes y' holds only for the pairs $a\to b$, $b\to c$, $c\to a$. Is $\forall x\,\exists y\,L(x,y)$ true? Is $\exists y\,\forall x\,L(x,y)$ true?
steps: $\forall x\,\exists y\,L(x,y)$: everyone likes someone. $a$ likes $b$, $b$ likes $c$, $c$ likes $a$. True.
$\exists y\,\forall x\,L(x,y)$: is there one person liked by everyone? Try $b$: only $a$ likes $b$. Try $c$: only $b$ likes $c$. Try $a$: only $c$ likes $a$. No one works. False.
Same symbols, swapped order, different truth value. In the first, the choice of $y$ may depend on $x$. In the second, one $y$ must serve every $x$.
examples.answer: The first is true and the second is false.

examples.setup: Translate 'every cat is a mammal' and 'some cat is black'. Why is $\exists x\,(\mathrm{Cat}(x)\to\mathrm{Black}(x))$ a bad translation of the second?
steps: All: $\forall x\,(\mathrm{Cat}(x)\to\mathrm{Mammal}(x))$. For each thing, if it is a cat then it is a mammal.
Some: $\exists x\,(\mathrm{Cat}(x)\wedge\mathrm{Black}(x))$. There is a thing that is a cat and black.
Try the bad form $\exists x\,(\mathrm{Cat}(x)\to\mathrm{Black}(x))$ in a world with one white cat and one dog.
For the dog, $\mathrm{Cat}$ is false, so the arrow is true. The bad statement is true, but no cat is black.
examples.answer: Use $\forall$ with $\to$ and $\exists$ with $\wedge$. The mixed form $\exists x\,(\mathrm{Cat}\to\mathrm{Black})$ is true even when no cat is black.

cards.why: Quantifiers let you state properties of whole collections: 'for every input the program halts', 'there is a path from s to t'. Negating them correctly is how proofs by counterexample work. In GATE: translating English into predicate logic, picking the correct negation, and judging which quantifier order is true.
how: Identify the domain and the predicates.
'All A are B' uses $\forall$ with $\to$. 'Some A is B' uses $\exists$ with $\wedge$.
To negate, flip $\forall$ and $\exists$ and negate the inside.
Read nested quantifiers left to right, as a game.
Test a tiny domain of 2 or 3 elements to check a claim.
cards.mistake: Negating 'every' as 'none' (a much stronger claim), swapping $\forall$ and $\exists$ without noticing the meaning changes, and translating with $\wedge$ under $\forall$ or $\to$ under $\exists$. One counterexample refutes 'for all', and one witness proves 'there exists'.
edge_cases: Over an empty domain, $\forall x\,P(x)$ is true and $\exists x\,P(x)$ is false.
$\exists y\,\forall x$ always implies $\forall x\,\exists y$, but not the other way round.
Two quantifiers of the same kind commute: $\forall x\,\forall y\equiv\forall y\,\forall x$.
A variable with no quantifier on it is free, and then the formula is not yet a statement.
connections: Used in: Discrete Maths. Predicate logic and its negation rules (dm.logic).
Used in: Theory of Computation. The pumping lemma has alternating quantifiers: there exists a length such that for all splittings (toc.langs_pumping).
Used in: Databases and AI. SQL uses EXISTS and NOT EXISTS, relational division is a 'for all', and first-order logic reasons with $\forall$ and $\exists$ (db.sql, db.relalg, ai.logic).

check.q: Negate: 'every bird can fly'.
Negate $\exists x\,(x>5)$.
Over the integers, is $\exists x\,\forall y\,(y\ge x)$ true?
check.a: No. There is no smallest integer, so no single $x$ works for every $y$.

scenes.title: Building all subsets of {a, b, c}: each new element doubles the count

steps.caption: With no elements there is exactly one subset: the empty set $\emptyset$. Count 1.
Add $a$. Every old subset can leave $a$ out or take it in, so we get $\emptyset$ and $\{a\}$. Count 2.
Add $b$ the same way: each old subset leaves $b$ out or takes it in. Count 4.
Add $c$: copy the 4 subsets and put $c$ into each copy. The new row holds $\{c\},\{a,c\},\{b,c\},\{a,b,c\}$. Count 8.
Each of the 3 elements is in or out, so the count is $2\times2\times2=2^3=8$.

scenes.title: Union, intersection, difference and complement on a Venn diagram

steps.caption: Draw the universe $U$ as a box and $A$, $B$ as overlapping circles. 1 and 2 are only in $A$, 3 and 4 are in both, 5 and 6 are only in $B$, and 7, 8, 9 are outside both circles.
Union $A\cup B$: light up everything inside either circle, which is $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$. The outside numbers fade.
Intersection $A\cap B$: only the overlap survives, $\{3,4\}$.
Difference $A-B$: inside $A$ but not in the overlap, $\{1,2\}$.
Complement $A'$: everything in the box outside circle $A$, which is $\{5,6,7,8,9\}$.

scenes.title: Two overlapping groups: fill the regions, then count

steps.caption: Draw a box of 40 students and two circles. Start in the overlap: 8 students play both games.
Cricket has 25 in total, and 8 of them sit in the overlap. Cricket only: $25-8=17$.
Football only: $18-8=10$.
At least one game: $17+8+10=35$. The shortcut $25+18-8=35$ gives the same, because the 8 were counted twice.
Neither: $40-35=5$, the students outside both circles.

scenes.title: p implies q as a promise: broken only when p is true and q is false

objects.text: p: it rains     q: I carry an umbrella
the promise: if it rains, I carry an umbrella

steps.caption: Four situations: rain or no rain, umbrella or no umbrella. The promise is 'if it rains, I carry an umbrella'.
Rain and umbrella (T, T): the promise is kept, so $p\to q=T$.
Rain and no umbrella (T, F): the promise is broken, so $p\to q=F$. This is the only false row.
No rain (F, T and F, F): nothing was promised, so nothing is broken. Both rows count as T.
Now compute $\neg p\vee q$ row by row: T, F, T, T. The two columns match, so $p\to q\equiv\neg p\vee q$.
